name: Hypoglycemia

matching.reasoningTemplate: Altered sensorium with low glucose is rapidly reversible and must be excluded first.

redFlags: Rapidly reversible — check glucose first in any altered patient

clinicalPearls: Symptoms fall into two groups: autonomic/adrenergic features (tremor, palpitations, anxiety, sweating, hunger, paresthesias) driven by counterregulatory activation, and neuroglycopenic features (fatigue, weakness, dizziness, confusion, behavioral change, cognitive impairment) from impaired neuronal function (p.204).
Hypoglycemia can cause transient loss of consciousness and may mimic syncope or seizure; hunger as a premonitory symptom and absence of immediate reorientation help distinguish it (p.204).
Insulinoma may first be misattributed to psychiatric illness, with symptoms (confusion, irrational behavior, visual difficulty, coma) recognized as neuroglycopenic only in retrospect (p.721).

Distinguish endogenous insulin excess (insulinoma) from surreptitious exogenous insulin use: C-peptide and proinsulin are elevated with insulinoma but suppressed with exogenous insulin injection (p.721).

A non-islet-cell tumor cause is suggested by hypoglycemia with suppressed insulin and C-peptide plus an elevated IGF-II/IGF-I ratio (>10:1) and inappropriately low GH and beta-hydroxybutyrate (p.635-636, p.782).
harrison.pathophysiology: Falling glucose triggers counterregulatory autonomic activation (catecholamines) producing adrenergic warning symptoms, while inadequate glucose supply to the brain produces neuroglycopenia. Endogenous hyperinsulinism (insulinoma) drives fasting hypoglycemia with elevated insulin, proinsulin, and C-peptide. Non-islet-cell tumors can cause hypoglycemia chiefly through secretion of incompletely processed IGF-II ('big' IGF-II), which weakly activates insulin receptors and more strongly IGF-I receptors; reduced IGFBP-3 and acid-labile subunit increase IGF-II bioavailability to target tissues, and large tumors may also impair hepatic gluconeogenesis or consume glucose. In severe malaria, hypoglycemia arises from failed hepatic gluconeogenesis combined with increased host (and to a lesser extent parasite) glucose consumption, and may be worsened by quinine-induced insulin secretion (p.204, p.635-636, p.721, p.782, p.1807).
additionalDifferentials: Insulinoma (endogenous hyperinsulinism) — fasting hypoglycemia with elevated insulin, proinsulin, C-peptide (p.721)
Surreptitious/factitious insulin or sulfonylurea use (suppressed C-peptide with exogenous insulin; serum sulfonylurea assay if suspected) (p.721)
Non-islet-cell tumor hypoglycemia from IGF-II excess (mesenchymal tumors, hepatomas, adrenocortical and other large tumors) (p.635-636, p.782)
Severe liver disease, alcoholism, and poor nutrition causing fasting hypoglycemia (p.721)
infectionMimics: Severe falciparum malaria — hypoglycemia is a common complication and its neurologic effects are indistinguishable from cerebral malaria; usual adrenergic signs (sweating, gooseflesh, tachycardia) are often absent (p.1807)
nonInfectiousMimics: Syncope and seizure — hypoglycemia-related loss of consciousness can be mistaken for either (p.204)
Psychiatric illness — neuroglycopenic behavioral symptoms of insulinoma can be misdiagnosed as psychiatric disease (p.721)

Pseudohypoglycemia — artifactually low glucose from in vitro glucose consumption by markedly elevated leukocytes (hyperleukocytosis in leukemia, myeloproliferative disease, leukemoid reaction, or after colony-stimulating factor) (p.635-636)
additionalInvestigations: C-peptide level — helps separate endogenous from exogenous insulin (p.721)
Serum/plasma sulfonylurea assay when surreptitious agent use suspected (p.721)
IGF-II level and IGF-II/IGF-I ratio (ratio >10:1 suggestive of non-islet-cell tumor hypoglycemia; standard IGF-II assays may miss precursors) (p.782)
Endoscopic ultrasound for localization of insulinoma (typically small, <2 cm) (p.721)
redFlags: Hypoglycemia complicating severe malaria carries a poor prognosis, especially in children and pregnant women, and the usual warning signs may be absent (p.1807)
Recurrent hypoglycemia blunts counterregulation, causing hypoglycemia unawareness — loss of the warning symptoms that normally prompt correction (p.204)
Coma or seizures from neuroglycopenia indicate severe, potentially irreversible CNS compromise (p.721, p.782)
harrison.prognosis: Hypoglycemia is rapidly reversible with glucose, but in severe malaria it independently signals a poor prognosis, particularly in children and pregnant women (p.1807).
pitfalls: Repeated hypoglycemia produces hypoglycemia unawareness by impairing the counterregulatory response, so the absence of adrenergic warning symptoms does not exclude dangerous hypoglycemia (p.204).

In severe malaria the clinical signs of hypoglycemia (sweating, gooseflesh, tachycardia) are typically absent and its neurologic effects mimic the underlying disease, so it is easily missed without glucose measurement (p.1807).
Failing to measure C-peptide/proinsulin can miss surreptitious exogenous insulin use, which mimics insulinoma (p.721).
Circulating IGF-II may not be overtly elevated in tumor-induced hypoglycemia, so a normal IGF-II level does not exclude it; the IGF-II/IGF-I ratio is more informative (p.635-636, p.782).
A markedly raised leukocyte count can cause artifactual low glucose (pseudohypoglycemia) if the sample is not processed promptly (p.635-636).
